questions.question: The passage primarily argues that:
questions.solution: The passage says repair 'has been priced out' (para 1), explains this through rising relative costs (para 2), and concludes that making repair cheaper beats making people feel guilty (paras 3–5). Option 1 is the view the author rejects ('not … consumer laziness'). Option 3 is described as how the rules are 'often described', and the author says their deeper effect is economic. Option 4 is never claimed: technicians work at the same speed, not with less skill.
options: consumers today repair less than earlier generations because they value their possessions less
the decline of repair is driven mainly by shifting relative prices, so policy should narrow the cost gap rather than appeal to values
right-to-repair rules are essentially consumer-protection measures
manufacturing efficiency has made repair technicians less skilled over time

questions.question: According to the passage, why has repair become relatively more expensive?
questions.solution: Paragraph 2: in low-productivity sectors 'wages must still keep pace with the rest of the economy, so prices rise', while manufacturing prices fall. A technician 'works at roughly the same speed … yet must be paid a modern wage'. There is no comparison of technicians' wages with factory wages (option 1). Supply chains are linked to cheap manufacturing, not missing parts (option 3). Consumer taste for features (option 4) is never mentioned.
options: Repair technicians now demand higher wages than factory workers
Repair productivity has barely changed, while wages must keep pace with an economy in which manufactured goods keep getting cheaper
Long supply chains have made spare parts impossible to obtain
Consumers increasingly prefer new models with more features

questions.question: With which of the following would the author most likely agree?
questions.solution: The author says 'moral appeals will achieve little' and lists lower taxes on repair among the 'more promising interventions' that 'target the price gap directly'. Option 1 contradicts this. Option 3 contradicts 'None of this means that culture is irrelevant'. Option 4 contradicts the claim that people sensibly 'respond to the costs in front of them'.
options: A public campaign urging people to cherish their belongings would substantially raise repair rates
A tax cut on repair services is likely to do more to increase repair than an awareness campaign
Cultural habits have no influence on whether people choose to repair
Households that replace broken appliances instead of repairing them are acting irrationally

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's argument?
questions.solution: The argument rests on prices being the main driver of repair decisions. If repair becoming cheaper changed nothing, that link is undercut. Options 2 and 3 are consistent with, and even support, the cost-disease explanation. Option 4 says nothing about whether prices drive behaviour.
options: In a region where subsidies made repair clearly cheaper than replacement, repair rates did not rise at all
Repair technicians' real wages have risen over the past fifty years
New appliances have become cheaper in real terms
Some manufacturers have lobbied against right-to-repair rules

questions.question: The example of the two drivers is used mainly to:
questions.solution: The paragraph ends: 'The only difference between them lies in something neither controlled', and the next paragraph names this 'moral luck'. The passage says nothing about the penalties being lenient (option 1). It never says the second driver is blameless (option 3). Option 4 is one view discussed later (the 'inner will' view), not the purpose of the example.
options: show that drink-driving penalties are too lenient
illustrate a case in which our judgements of blame seem to depend on something outside the agents' control
argue that the second driver deserves no blame at all
demonstrate that intentions matter more than outcomes

questions.question: According to the passage, the main difficulty with applying the control principle consistently is that it:
questions.solution: Paragraph 3: the principle 'threatens to swallow almost everything' (temperament, upbringing, circumstances), and 'it is not obvious that anything remains to be judged'. Option 3 is the reverse: the principle focuses on what we control, including intentions. Options 1 and 4 concern the law, which isn't the stated difficulty.
options: would make the law too harsh on careless drivers
would leave little or nothing open to moral judgement, since so much that shapes us is beyond our control
cannot account for the intentions of agents
conflicts with the way courts assign penalties

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the view that only the 'inner will' should be judged is best described as:
questions.solution: 'This view has the merit of consistency, but it struggles to explain experiences that seem central to moral life.' The author grants a strength (so not contempt), raises a serious objection (so not endorsement), and clearly evaluates it (so not neutral).
options: wholehearted endorsement
acknowledging its consistency while doubting that it fits our moral experience
dismissive contempt
strict neutrality, offering no evaluation

questions.question: Which of the following can best be inferred about the author's own position?
questions.solution: The final paragraph presents acceptance sympathetically and ends by suggesting that 'the demand that morality be perfectly fair was itself a fantasy', which signals agreement. Option 1 is the view the author resists. Option 3 has no support. Option 4 contradicts 'The second driver will rightly feel something'.
options: The author thinks moral luck should be eliminated from our moral practices
The author leans towards accepting moral luck, even if this makes morality less tidy and less fair
The author believes the first driver is more blameworthy than the second
The author regards the second driver's regret as irrational

questions.question: According to the passage, the replication crisis is mainly explained by:
questions.solution: Paragraph 2: 'deliberate fabrication explains only a small part', and 'the deeper causes are structural': journals preferring striking results, plus 'many small decisions' that can 'make chance patterns look like real discoveries'. Options 3 and 4 are never mentioned.
options: widespread deliberate fabrication of data
publication incentives and many small analytical choices that can make chance patterns look like real findings
outdated laboratory equipment
journals refusing to publish psychology research

questions.question: Which of the following statements about statistical significance is consistent with the passage?
questions.solution: Paragraph 3 says this almost word for word. Option 1 is the misreading the passage warns against. Option 3 contradicts 'The statistical threshold itself has come in for criticism' and the role of nudging results 'across the conventional threshold'. Option 4 is the reverse of the final sentence of paragraph 3.
options: A significant result means there is at most a five per cent chance that the finding is false
Whether a significant result reflects a real effect depends partly on the hypothesis's prior plausibility and the study's statistical power
Significance thresholds played no role in the replication crisis
Testing many hypotheses in small samples makes false alarms rarer

questions.question: As described in the passage, the main purpose of a registered report is to:
questions.solution: The journal agrees to publish 'on the strength of its design, before the results are known, removing the incentive to produce a striking outcome'. Speed (option 1) isn't mentioned. Option 3 is what preregistration prevents. Option 4 is never stated.
options: speed up the publication of results
make the decision to publish independent of whether the results turn out to be striking
allow researchers to revise their analysis after seeing the data
replace peer review with public registration

questions.question: The reformers' reply in the final paragraph implies that:
questions.solution: 'The aim is not to forbid researchers from following hunches, but to stop hunches confirmed after the fact from being presented as predictions made in advance.' Option 1 contradicts 'exploration is welcome'. Option 3 contradicts the critics' point that exploration 'often precedes genuine breakthroughs', which the reformers don't dispute. Option 4 isn't stated.
options: exploratory research should be discouraged
the problem is not exploration itself but presenting after-the-fact findings as if they had been predicted
hunches rarely lead to genuine breakthroughs
critics have misunderstood the statistics behind preregistration

questions.question: The author's central claim is that:
questions.solution: The final paragraph states the author's conclusion: 'A translation is better understood as a reading', and many translations are 'evidence of the poem's richness'. Option 1 is called 'an exaggeration'. Option 2 ignores the failures of strict fidelity the author describes. Option 4 is only one method mentioned in paragraph 4, never a universal rule.
options: poetry cannot be translated in any meaningful sense
literal translations are always preferable to free ones
a translation is best seen as one partial reading rather than a replacement, so many translations reflect a poem's richness rather than failure
translators should always add explanatory notes

questions.question: The 'pressed flower' comparison suggests that strictly faithful translations can:
questions.solution: Such translations are 'accurate in every particular and lifeless as a whole', like a flower keeping 'the shape of a bloom but none of its scent'. Option 1 contradicts 'accurate in every particular'. Options 3 and 4 have no support.
options: contain errors of detail
keep a poem's form and particulars while losing its living effect
become more beautiful than the original
be impossible for ordinary readers to understand

questions.question: What does the passage suggest about translations admired 'as poems in their own right'?
questions.solution: Such admiration is 'both a tribute to the translator and a quiet admission of distance from the source'. Option 1 is the opposite. Option 3 contradicts 'celebrated'. Option 4 describes the third approach, which is a different method.
options: They prove that the translator stayed closest to the original
Their being admired in this way hints that they may have moved away from the source poem
They are rarely successful with readers
They usually print the original and a literal version side by side

questions.question: Which of the following would the author most likely consider an honest way of dealing with what is lost in translation?
questions.solution: Paragraph 4 says these methods 'treat the loss honestly rather than disguising it'. Options 1 and 4 disguise changes. Option 3 avoids the problem rather than dealing with it, and the passage never suggests it.
options: Presenting a free recreation without mentioning the original's wordplay
Publishing the original with a literal and a freer version, along with notes on puns and allusions
Translating only poems that contain no wordplay
Updating the poem's imagery for modern readers without comment

questions.question:
The four sentences below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Enter the sequence of the four numbers (e.g. 2143).

  1. These inventions were not always idle decoration; some, copied from map to map, sent later sailors in search of lands that did not exist.
  2. The first printed maps of the world were as much works of imagination as of measurement.
  3. Only with better instruments and systematic surveys did the blank spaces come to be admitted honestly as unknown.
  4. Where explorers had not yet reached, mapmakers filled the gaps with sea monsters, mythical islands and confident guesses.
questions.solution: Correct order: 2413. The opener introduces imaginative maps. 'Where explorers had not yet reached…' explains how gaps were filled. 'These inventions' must follow the inventions (monsters, islands). 'Only with better instruments…' closes the history.

questions.question:
The four sentences below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Enter the sequence of the four numbers (e.g. 2143).

  1. Yet they perform measurable work: shading pavements, absorbing rainwater and cooling the air around them.
  2. Putting a money value on that work has persuaded some councils to protect trees they once saw as expendable.
  3. A city's street trees are often treated as ornaments, planted for beauty and removed when inconvenient.
  4. On hot afternoons, a tree-lined street can be noticeably cooler than a bare one a few blocks away.
questions.solution: Correct order: 3142. The 'ornament' view comes first. 'Yet' introduces the contrast (they do work). The hot-afternoon example illustrates the cooling. 'That work' in the last sentence refers back to the work described, so it comes last.

questions.question:
The four sentences below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Enter the sequence of the four numbers (e.g. 2143).

  1. Longer-playing formats eventually removed the limit.
  2. Musicians adapted, trimming and arranging their pieces to fit within that span.
  3. Yet the habit it had created proved durable, and the short pop song outlived the technology that shaped it.
  4. Early gramophone records could hold only about three minutes of music per side.
questions.solution: Correct order: 4213. Constraint → adaptation → the limit removed → 'Yet the habit it had created' ('it' = the limit), which needs the removal sentence just before it.

questions.question:
The four sentences below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Enter the sequence of the four numbers (e.g. 2143).

  1. Honeybees tell their nest-mates where food is through a movement known as the waggle dance.
  2. Together, these two cues let other foragers fly straight to a source they have never visited.
  3. The angle of the dance relative to the vertical indicates the direction of the food relative to the sun.
  4. The duration of the waggling run, meanwhile, signals how far away the food is.
questions.solution: Correct order: 1342. Introduce the dance, then cue 1 (angle = direction), then 'meanwhile' cue 2 (duration = distance), then 'Together, these two cues' summarises both.

questions.question:
The four sentences below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Enter the sequence of the four numbers (e.g. 2143).

  1. The reasoning was that capital would flow to where it was scarce and earned the highest returns.
  2. In the 1950s and 1960s, many economists expected poorer countries to catch up steadily with richer ones.
  3. In practice, convergence happened in some regions but not in others, and the gap sometimes widened.
  4. This mixed record pushed researchers to look beyond capital, towards institutions, education and geography.
questions.solution: Correct order: 2134. Expectation → 'The reasoning was…' (explains the expectation) → 'In practice…' (contrast with reality) → 'This mixed record…' (consequence).

questions.question:
The four sentences below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Enter the sequence of the four numbers (e.g. 2143).

  1. The machines, in other words, ended up raising human standards rather than replacing human interest.
  2. Instead, players began using the programs as training partners, and the standard of top-level play rose.
  3. Many feared that this would leave the game pointless for people.
  4. Chess programs now play far better than any human champion.
questions.solution: Correct order: 4321. Fact → fear ('this' = machines being better) → 'Instead…' (what actually happened) → 'in other words' summarises the outcome.

questions.question:
Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Remote work was once imagined as a perk for a few; it is now a structural feature of many industries. Its advantages are real: saved commuting time, wider hiring pools and greater flexibility for carers. But organisations have discovered costs that are harder to measure. Newcomers learn more slowly when they cannot watch experienced colleagues, and the informal exchanges that spark ideas become rarer. The firms that seem to be adapting best are not those that have chosen one model wholesale, but those that decide deliberately which activities need people together and which do not.
questions.solution: The paragraph weighs real benefits against harder-to-measure costs and ends with its main point: the best firms decide deliberately activity by activity. Option 1 contradicts 'advantages are real'. Option 3 picks out one detail and turns it into a rule. Option 4 misreads one listed benefit as the cause.
options: Remote work has more costs than benefits, so firms should return to the office.
Remote work brings clear benefits but subtler costs, and organisations do best by deliberately matching each activity to the right setting.
New employees should always work from the office.
Remote work spread mainly because of the needs of carers.

questions.question:
Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Languages rarely die because they are banned. More often they fade through quiet calculation. When parents conclude that their children's prospects depend on a dominant language, they speak it at home, and within a generation or two the older tongue survives mainly among the elderly. Efforts at revival therefore succeed less through nostalgia than through making the language useful again, in schools, media, local government and work.
questions.solution: Both the cause (practical calculation by parents) and the remedy (usefulness, not nostalgia) are captured only by option 2. Option 1 contradicts the first sentence. Option 4 contradicts the last sentence. Option 3 is not claimed.
options: Languages mainly disappear because governments ban them.
Language loss is driven largely by families' practical choices, so revival depends on making the language practically useful again.
Elderly speakers bear the main responsibility for keeping languages alive.
Nostalgia is the strongest force behind successful language revival.

questions.question:
Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

A well-designed default can shape behaviour as powerfully as a rule. When employees are automatically enrolled in a pension scheme and must opt out, participation is far higher than when they must actively opt in, even though the choice on offer is identical. Defaults work because people tend to stay with whatever requires no action. That gives the designers of forms and systems a quiet but considerable power, and with it a responsibility to set defaults in people's interest.
questions.solution: The paragraph moves from evidence (auto-enrolment) to mechanism (inertia) to conclusion (power and responsibility). Option 2 has all three. Option 1 isn't argued. Option 3 overstates 'as powerfully as'. Option 4 is never stated: the point is inertia, not indifference.
options: Pension schemes should be made compulsory for all employees.
Because people tend to stick with defaults, those who set them hold real influence and should use it in people's interest.
Defaults are more effective than laws in every situation.
Most employees are indifferent to their pensions.

questions.question:
Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Museums once displayed objects taken from colonies with little comment on how they had been acquired. Today many institutions add information about provenance, and some have returned items to the communities they came from. Critics say this politicises collections. Supporters reply that silence about origins was always a political choice too, merely an unexamined one.
questions.solution: The paragraph describes a change in practice and the debate about it, ending with the supporters' rebuttal. Option 2 covers both sides accurately. Option 1 takes a position the paragraph doesn't. Options 3 and 4 are unsupported.
options: Museums should return every object acquired during the colonial era.
As museums add context about colonial-era objects, critics call this political, while supporters argue that the earlier silence was itself political.
Critics have stopped museums from returning objects to their places of origin.
Provenance information is of little interest to museum visitors.

questions.question:
Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Sleep is often treated as time lost to productivity. Yet research on learning suggests that memories formed during the day are strengthened and reorganised during sleep, and that people deprived of it perform worse on tasks requiring both recall and judgement. Cutting sleep to gain working hours may therefore lower the quality of the very work it is meant to increase.
questions.solution: The paragraph's conclusion ('therefore…') is that cutting sleep can backfire on work quality because sleep supports memory and judgement. That is option 2. Option 1 gives a specific figure that isn't in the text. Options 3 and 4 are unrelated claims.
options: Everyone should sleep for more than eight hours a night.
Because sleep supports memory and judgement, giving it up for extra working time can undermine the work itself.
Sleep matters more than learning.
Productivity is impossible to measure accurately.

questions.question:
Five jumbled sentences are given. Four of them can form a coherent paragraph. Enter the number of the sentence that does not fit.

  1. Coral reefs cover a tiny fraction of the ocean floor yet support a remarkably large share of marine species.
  2. Their structure is built by colonies of small animals that secrete skeletons of calcium carbonate.
  3. Rising sea temperatures can cause corals to expel the algae living in their tissues, leaving them bleached.
  4. Deep-sea trenches remain among the least explored places on Earth.
  5. Repeated bleaching gives reefs too little time to recover, threatening the many species that depend on them.
questions.solution: Odd sentence: 4. Sentences 1, 2, 3 and 5 build a paragraph about coral reefs: their importance, their structure, bleaching, and its consequences. The deep-sea trenches sentence is about a different marine environment.

questions.question:
Five jumbled sentences are given. Four of them can form a coherent paragraph. Enter the number of the sentence that does not fit.

  1. Street food in many Indian cities is sold from carts that move with the rhythms of the day.
  2. The Indian Railways is one of the largest employers in the world.
  3. Breakfast vendors appear near railway stations early in the morning, and chaat sellers gather near markets in the evening.
  4. Office districts draw lunchtime stalls that vanish by late afternoon.
  5. This mobility lets vendors follow their customers rather than wait for customers to find them.
questions.solution: Odd sentence: 2. The paragraph is about vendors moving through the day to follow customers (morning, lunch, evening, then 'This mobility'). The railways-as-employer sentence picks up the word 'railway' but is off-topic.

questions.question:
Five jumbled sentences are given. Four of them can form a coherent paragraph. Enter the number of the sentence that does not fit.

  1. The printing press made books far cheaper to produce.
  2. As prices fell, reading spread beyond clergy and scholars to merchants and artisans.
  3. Many medieval manuscripts were decorated with gold leaf.
  4. Wider literacy in turn created demand for pamphlets, almanacs and news sheets.
  5. Within a few generations, printed material had changed how ideas circulated across Europe.
questions.solution: Odd sentence: 3. Sentences 1, 2, 4 and 5 form a cause-and-effect chain: cheaper books → wider reading → demand for new print → changed circulation of ideas. The gold-leaf sentence describes manuscript decoration and breaks the chain.

questions.question:
Five jumbled sentences are given. Four of them can form a coherent paragraph. Enter the number of the sentence that does not fit.

  1. Penguins cannot fly but are strong swimmers.
  2. Many birds migrate thousands of kilometres every year.
  3. They navigate using several cues, including the positions of the sun and stars.
  4. Some species also appear able to sense the Earth's magnetic field.
  5. In some species, young birds on their first journey follow experienced adults and learn the route as they go.
questions.solution: Odd sentence: 1. Sentences 2–5 explain how migrating birds find their way: celestial cues, magnetism, learning from adults. The penguin sentence is about a flightless bird's swimming and has nothing to do with navigation.

questions.question: The author's central claim about queues is that they:
questions.solution: Para 7 states the conclusion: queues plainly waste time, but where a community values "a visible and equal rule" more than the time, they should be shortened, not abolished. Option 1 contradicts "None of this makes queues efficient". Option 4 is the economists' view the author qualifies. Option 3 reverses para 3, where hiring stand-ins makes the fairness claim "collapse".
options: are an efficient way of allocating goods that markets cannot price
waste time but can be justified where a visible, equal rule of allocation is valued
are fair only when people are allowed to hire others to wait for them
should be replaced by fees wherever a community can agree on a fair price

questions.question: According to the passage, why do queues persist for goods such as emergency care?
questions.solution: Para 2: a queue charges "in a currency that is distributed with rough equality", which is why it persists for goods treated as "matters of fairness". Option 2 is never said. Option 1 misrepresents the economists, who think prices are too low. Option 4 contradicts para 3.
options: Because economists have shown that prices would be set too high
Because such goods cannot be produced in larger quantities
Because waiting charges everyone in a currency that is distributed roughly equally
Because people who need such goods most have the most free time

questions.question: The author would most likely regard a system in which wealthy patients pay agents to hold their place in a hospital queue as:
questions.solution: Para 3: when people hire stand-ins, the queue "rations by the wages of the stand-ins, and its claim to fairness collapses", i.e. money has re-entered. Option 2 is not endorsed; the author says fairness collapses. Option 1 does not follow; the case, if anything, strengthens the role of money. Option 3 is unsupported: nothing suggests paid place-holding is more legible.
options: proof that the economists' original criticism of queues was mistaken
a reasonable compromise between efficiency and fairness
a more legible system than an ordinary queue
evidence that the queue has become a disguised form of price rationing

questions.question: The contrast between "the surgeon" and "the retired clerk" in paragraph 2 serves mainly to:
questions.solution: The example follows "it assumes that money and time are interchangeable for everyone at the same rate. They are not." It illustrates unequal money-value of time against equal stocks of time. Options 3, 2 and 4 draw conclusions the passage never makes.
options: illustrate that time and money are not exchanged at the same rate by everyone
argue that surgeons should be given priority in public queues
show that professionals are less patient than retired people
suggest that queues discriminate against older people

questions.question: According to the passage, proponents consider planting locally collected seed risky because:
questions.solution: Para 2: local seed "is adapted to a past that will not return", while a tree must suit the climates "it will meet over its life". Option 3 inverts the critics' concern about moved seed. Option 2 is not stated. Option 4 is the critics' objection to assisted migration, not the proponents' reason.
options: such seed is adapted to climatic conditions that will not persist over the tree's life
local populations grow more slowly than southern ones
local seed is often contaminated with fungi and insects
climate models are unreliable about local conditions

questions.question: The author's comment that the proponents' reply "quietly changes the goal" implies that:
questions.solution: Para 4: a mixed planting is "a hedge against not knowing which tree is right", so the reply implicitly accepts uncertainty about the right match. Option 4 over-reads "quietly"; no deception is alleged. Option 2 contradicts "That may well be wise". Option 1 contradicts "a lower expected growth".
options: diversity in plantings increases expected growth
the reply is unsound and should be rejected
the reply concedes that the precise best match of tree to site cannot be known in advance
mixed plantings are a form of deception by foresters

questions.question: Which best describes the organisation of the passage?
questions.solution: Paras 1–2 give the problem and proposal, para 3 two objections, para 4 a reply and its cost, para 5 says the second objection is "harder to answer". Option 3 overstates: no experiment refutes anything. Option 2 mentions only para 1's background. Option 4 ignores the objections.
options: A problem is stated, a solution proposed, objections raised, a reply assessed, and one objection judged more serious
Two historical periods are compared to predict a future trend
A theory is introduced and then refuted by experimental evidence
A policy is described and its benefits are listed in order of importance

questions.question: The author's final paragraph relies on which of the following assumptions?
questions.solution: The claim that costs "are not confined to the plantation" only holds if what travels with the seed can spread beyond the stand. Option 3 attributes a motive the author never suggests; the point is about authority to choose, not indifference. Option 2 is wrong: para 4 says mixing lowers, not eliminates, risk, and it concerns the first objection. Option 4 contradicts the passage's premise that conditions are shifting.
options: Organisms introduced with moved seed may spread beyond the planted stand
Mixed plantings eliminate the risks posed by climate forecasting errors
Foresters are generally indifferent to the health of neighbouring woodland
Local woodland is already adapted to the climate projected for this century

questions.question: The passage is primarily concerned with arguing that:
questions.solution: The passage moves from "more like editing" (para 1) through the limits of both rules to "turns the unveiling from a claim of truth into an argument" (para 4). Option 1 is never argued. Option 3 misreads para 2, which says instruments reveal composition, not intention, not that they are unreliable. Option 2 is one view the author criticises in para 3.
options: restorers should never clean old paintings
patina should always be preserved because it is historically truthful
the instruments used in restoration are unreliable
restoration involves interpretive choices and should be presented as argument rather than revelation

questions.question: The author's point about the "thin brown layer" is that:
questions.solution: Para 2: "the instruments can tell us its composition, not its intention." Options 4 and 1 each assert one interpretation the author says is open. Option 2 is not stated.
options: it proves the artist added glazes late
restorers usually ignore such layers
technical analysis can identify what it is made of but not why it was applied
it is always a later varnish and can safely be removed

questions.question: The author's objection to the patina position is that:
questions.solution: Para 3: patina "is not neutral either": it can obscure intended details and create effects wrongly attributed to the painter. Option 2 trivialises the point. Option 3 is not raised. Option 4 contradicts the author's acknowledgement that patina records the work's life.
options: patina may itself distort the work, so preserving it is also a choice with consequences
patina makes ceilings too dark for modern visitors
patina is impossible to measure
patina has no historical value

questions.question: Which practice would the author most likely endorse?
questions.solution: Para 6 recommends publishing "what was removed, why, and on what evidence" so the result becomes "an argument that others can examine". Option 2 is the "revelation" framing rejected. Option 3 goes beyond the author, who criticises presentation, not cleaning itself. Option 4 replaces evidence with a vote; the passage asks for examinable reasons, not popularity.
options: Publishing a report listing which layers were removed, the evidence for each decision, and the uncertainties that remain
Unveiling a cleaned fresco with the claim that visitors now see it exactly as the artist intended
Leaving a darkened fresco untouched because any cleaning is dishonest
Asking the public to vote on which layers should be removed

questions.question: The author's main purpose is to:
questions.solution: Para 1 redefines regret as a judgement "by the lights of values one still holds"; para 2 concludes it is "not irrational but answerable to reasons". Option 3 is the practical advice the author partly grants but does not argue for. Option 2 overstates an analogy. Option 4 contradicts para 5.
options: argue that regret is a value-relative judgement and can therefore be rational
show that historians and individuals judge the past in identical ways
advise readers to stop dwelling on past mistakes
prove that values never change

questions.question: Which case would the author regard as an instance of irrational regret?
questions.solution: The last sentence: irrational regret is regret that tracks "a value one has openly abandoned". Option 3 fits exactly. Option 4 is the passage's model of rational regret. Option 2 is the author's own example of legitimate change (para 5). Option 1 is a trap: it involves outcomes, but nothing establishes that the regret tracks no value; it is underspecified rather than clearly irrational.
options: A person regrets missing a train though the missed journey turned out badly for others
A person's regret over a career choice fades as her priorities change
A person who has openly given up caring about social status still regrets not attending a prestigious party
A person regrets a cruel remark because she still values kindness

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's reply in the final paragraph?
questions.solution: The reply depends on "values are not moods" but "relatively stable commitments". If values shifted within days with feelings, the worry that the past becomes "hostage to our moods" would return. Option 3 is about new facts, consistent with the author. Option 4 concerns individuals, not the argument's premise. Option 2 is irrelevant to whether regret is reason-answerable.
options: People's reported values frequently shift within days in response to passing feelings
Regret is often accompanied by physical symptoms of distress
Historians sometimes revise their judgements when new documents are found
Some people feel little regret about anything

questions.question: The analogy with the historian in the last paragraph is used to suggest that:
questions.solution: The historian's judgement changes "when she comes to care about questions her predecessors ignored", which is "no more scandalous" than value-driven reassessment of one's own past. Option 2 is literal misreading. Option 3 reverses the point: the analogy defends such shifts as reasoned. Option 4 contradicts "The past act is unchanged".
options: reassessing the past because one's questions or commitments have changed is a normal feature of reasoned judgement
personal histories should be written by professional historians
historians are as unreliable as individuals in judging the past
the facts of the past are constantly changing

questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Libraries that lend tools, seeds or musical instruments are sometimes treated as charming novelties. Yet they rest on the same logic as the book library: many objects are used rarely, owning them individually ties up money and space, and a shared stock allows more people to use more things. The obstacles are practical rather than conceptual: objects break, need cleaning and are harder to catalogue than books.
questions.solution: The passage claims shared logic and practical, not conceptual, obstacles. Option 3 contradicts it, option 2 is not proposed, option 4 is not stated.
options: Libraries of things apply the same rationale as book libraries; their difficulties lie in handling the objects, not in the idea.
Book libraries should stop lending books and lend tools instead.
Lending libraries for tools and seeds are a passing trend that will fade.
Most people prefer to own tools rather than borrow them.

questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

When a city publishes the average commute time, it invites residents to compare their own journeys with a number that may describe almost no one. A city where half the workers live next to their offices and half travel ninety minutes has an average of forty-five minutes, yet nobody commutes for forty-five minutes. Averages are useful for budgets, which add up, but misleading for experiences, which do not.
questions.solution: The example shows an average describing no one; the last sentence contrasts budgets with experiences. Option 2 alleges miscalculation, but the arithmetic is fine. Option 4 is an unstated recommendation. Option 1 is a detail of a hypothetical.
options: Most workers in large cities live close to their offices.
Average commute figures are calculated incorrectly by most cities.
An average may suit aggregate purposes such as budgeting while misrepresenting individual experience, especially when the distribution is split.
Cities should stop publishing statistics on commuting.

questions.question:
There is a sentence that is missing in the paragraph below. Read the paragraph and choose the option that best completes it.

Early mapmakers in many traditions placed their own city at the centre of the world. It is easy to smile at this, but modern digital maps do something similar more subtly: they centre the map on the user's location and enlarge the streets nearest to her. ____ The difference is that the older maps announced their bias, while ours present it as a neutral service.
questions.solution: The blank must generalise the user-centred map before the "difference" sentence contrasts old and new bias. Option 4 does this. Option 1 changes the subject to accuracy. Option 3 conflicts with "It is easy to smile at this, but". Option 2 contradicts the claim that digital maps do centre.
options: Digital maps are therefore far more accurate than older maps.
Satellite imaging has made such centring unnecessary.
Older mapmakers were simply ignorant of geography.
Every user, in effect, now lives at the centre of her own world.

questions.question:
There is a sentence that is missing in the paragraph below. Read the paragraph and choose the option that best completes it.

Committees are often blamed for producing cautious decisions, as if caution were a defect of character spread across several people. A more structural explanation is available. Each member can be blamed for a bold proposal that fails, but no one is singled out when a modest proposal merely disappoints. ____ The remedy, if one is wanted, lies less in recruiting braver members than in changing who is held responsible for what.
questions.solution: The blank must sum up the structural explanation and set up the "remedy" about responsibility. Option 1 does so. Option 2 is a remedy the final sentence does not support. Option 4 reverts to the character explanation the paragraph rejects. Option 3 is an absolute claim the paragraph never makes; it concerns blame, not failure rates.
options: Caution, in other words, is what an arrangement of individual blame and shared credit rationally produces.
Committees should therefore be abolished in favour of single decision-makers.
Bold proposals always fail more often than modest ones.
Most committee members are naturally timid people.

questions.question:
Five jumbled sentences related to a topic are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd one out and key in its number.

  1. A bridge's designers must allow for loads it may meet only once in a century.
  2. Such rare loads, a record flood or an unusual crowd, matter more to its safety than daily traffic.
  3. Engineers therefore design for extremes rather than averages.
  4. Daily traffic, by contrast, determines how quickly a bridge's deck wears and must be resurfaced.
  5. The result can look wasteful in ordinary years, which is precisely when it is doing its job.
questions.solution: Sentences 1, 2, 3 and 5 form a chain about designing for rare extremes. Sentence 4 is about routine wear and maintenance, a bridge topic but a different concern from designing for rare extremes.

questions.question:
Five jumbled sentences related to a topic are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd one out and key in its number.

  1. Translators of legal texts face a problem that literary translators rarely do: a mistranslated term can change who owns what.
  2. A word for "property" in one system may include rights that another system treats separately.
  3. For this reason, legal translators often keep the original term and add a gloss rather than choose a near equivalent.
  4. Literary translators, by contrast, are prized for finding equivalents that feel natural to readers.
  5. Legal language has grown steadily more complex over the past century.
questions.solution: 1 sets the problem, 2 explains it, 3 gives the legal translator's response, and 4 contrasts literary practice, picking up 1's comparison. Sentence 5 makes a general claim about complexity over time that nothing else develops. Sentence 4 may look like a digression, but it completes the contrast opened in 1.

questions.question:
The four sentences below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Enter the sequence of the four numbers (e.g. 2143).

  1. This silence was not an accident of record-keeping.
  2. Household accounts from the period list the price of candles, flour and cloth, but almost never the hours of labour that turned them into meals and clothing.
  3. Labour done inside the home was simply not thought of as work that could be counted.
  4. Historians who want to measure domestic work must therefore reconstruct it from diaries and court testimony.
questions.solution: 2 introduces the evidence (accounts omit labour). 1 refers back to it as "This silence". 3 explains why. 4 draws the consequence with "therefore". 1 cannot open, since "This silence" needs an antecedent.

questions.question:
The five sentences below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Enter the sequence of the five numbers (e.g. 21435).

  1. That expectation, however, assumes that people read labels when they choose.
  2. Food labels were introduced on the expectation that informed shoppers would choose healthier products.
  3. Studies of supermarket behaviour suggest that most choices take a few seconds and rely on habit.
  4. If labels work at all, then, they may do so less by informing shoppers than by prompting manufacturers to reformulate products they would rather not advertise.
  5. In such conditions, a label is less a source of information than background noise.
questions.solution: 2 states the original expectation. 1 ("That expectation, however") questions its assumption. 3 supplies the evidence. 5 ("In such conditions") draws the implication. 4 ("then") concludes with the alternative mechanism.

questions.question: The passage is primarily concerned with:
questions.solution: The author lists documentary, legal and claimant obstacles and closes that a debate treating repatriation "as a test of moral courage alone" misdirects pressure. Option 3 overstates; the author never says acquisitions were lawful. Option 2 is not advocated. Option 1 is one supporting detail.
options: describing the history of record-keeping in national museums
arguing that all disputed museum objects should be returned to their countries of origin
defending museums against the charge that they acquired objects unlawfully
explaining why the return of museum objects is slower than a moral framing of the debate suggests

questions.question: According to the passage, a curator who believes an object should be returned may be unable to return it because:
questions.solution: Para 3: objects "belong to the state and may be removed ... only by an act of the legislature", so curators "may be forbidden from sending it". Options 4 and 3 are separate obstacles, not why a persuaded curator is blocked. Option 1 misuses the insurance detail from para 2.
options: the museum would lose insurance coverage on its collection
the object legally belongs to the state and its removal requires legislative action
more than one community claims the object
the object's ownership records are incomplete

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim about where critics direct their pressure?
questions.solution: The author says critics misread delays because the people addressed "often lack the power to say yes". If directors do have that power and decline, pressure on them is well aimed. Options 3, 1 and 2 restate obstacles the author already accepts, which would strengthen rather than weaken the argument.
options: Many claims are made by more than one community.
Research into an object's provenance often takes several years.
Most national museums keep acquisition records only for insurance purposes.
In several countries, museum directors can deaccession objects on their own authority but routinely decline to.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the critics of museums is best described as:
questions.solution: The final paragraph refuses to let museums "proceed at their own pace" (sympathy with the goal) but faults a debate that "directs its pressure at the wrong people". Option 3 ignores that sympathy, option 1 ignores the criticism, and option 2 contradicts the engaged conclusion.
options: wholly supportive of their methods
indifferent to the outcome of the debate
dismissive, regarding their demands as unjustified
sympathetic to their goal but critical of how they frame and target the issue

questions.question: According to the passage, the water table in a newly pumped region may remain stable for years because:
questions.solution: Para 2: the level "may barely move for years, because the aquifer is drawing on stored water". Options 3, 2 and 1 are not given as reasons.
options: recharge schemes replace the water being withdrawn
officials restrict pumping during the first years
rainfall typically increases when pumping begins
the aquifer is initially drawing on water stored over a long period

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author regards the "share of the aquifer's estimated safe yield" approach as valuable mainly because it:
questions.solution: The approach makes restraint "a protection of one's own entitlement" and "aligns the time horizon of the individual with that of the resource". Option 1 overstates; "the results are mixed". Option 3 is wrong because shares depend on "estimated safe yield". Option 4 is not discussed.
options: guarantees that aquifers will not be depleted
gives individual users a reason to conserve that serves their own long-term interest
removes the need for hydrologists' estimates
allows elected officials to avoid unpopular decisions

questions.question: The third paragraph serves to:
questions.solution: Para 3 opens "The same delay works in the other direction" and shows that cuts and recharge show results too late to sustain political will. Option 3 confuses delayed benefits with no benefits. Options 4 and 1 are unsupported.
options: recommend that elected officials be replaced by hydrologists
show that the time lag also undermines efforts at recovery, not only the detection of overuse
argue that recharge schemes are ineffective
introduce a new cause of well failure

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the author's view of uncertainty in hydrological projections?
questions.solution: Para 5: uncertainty "tends to be resolved in favour of present use", and "What is lacking is less information than an institution". Option 1 contradicts "less information". Options 4 and 3 go further than the author, who proposes an institutional response.
options: It is the main reason aquifers are overused, and better data would solve the problem.
In practice it is used to justify continued extraction, so the deeper deficit is institutional rather than informational.
It is unavoidable and therefore no policy response is possible.
It makes projections worthless and they should be abandoned.

questions.question: The author's main argument is that:
questions.solution: Para 2 argues that concepts can be explained; para 3 locates "the more serious difficulty" in associations; para 4 sums up that the lists exaggerate the conceptual gulf and understate the gulf in texture. Option 4 is the view rejected. Option 2 is not advised. Option 3 imputes intent; the lists "mislead" but are not called deliberate.
options: the real challenge of translation lies in conveying associations and texture, not in finding equivalents for supposedly untranslatable concepts
translators should avoid words with strong associations
lists of untranslatable words are deliberately misleading
untranslatable words prove that speakers of different languages think differently

questions.question: According to the author, what a second language lacks when it has no single word for a concept is:
questions.solution: Para 2: "What is missing in the second language is not the concept but its compression: a ready-made unit". Option 1 is denied. Option 4 belongs to the discussion in para 3. Option 3 is never mentioned.
options: the ability to express the concept at all
a compressed, ready-made unit for the concept
speakers who are interested in the concept
the associations the concept carries in poetry

questions.question: The example of the word for "home" is used to show that:
questions.solution: It follows "it arises with ordinary vocabulary as much as with exotic terms": a common word differs in tone across languages. Option 3 is false; both languages have the word. Options 1 and 4 generalise beyond the example.
options: bureaucratic language is harder to translate than poetry
problems of tone and association affect even common words, not only exotic ones
some languages have no word for home
tender words cannot be translated accurately

questions.question: Which of the following situations best illustrates what the author calls the gulf at "the level of texture"?
questions.solution: Para 6: at the level of texture "a translation can be accurate in every sentence and still feel like a different work". Option 4 matches this exactly. Option 2 is the conceptual gap the author says explanation bridges. Options 3 and 1 are irrelevant.
options: Two dictionaries give different definitions for the same word.
A reader cannot understand a foreign term until it is explained in a footnote.
A language invents a new word for a newly discovered substance.
A novel's translation conveys every event and statement correctly, yet readers of the original find its humour and formality strangely altered.

questions.question: Which of the following best states the central point of the passage?
questions.solution: The passage credits benchmarks' virtues, explains their decay, recommends corroboration, and concludes with "measures whose limits are acknowledged". Option 2 contradicts "It would be wrong to conclude that benchmarks are a mistake" and "No one need cheat". Option 3 contradicts para 4. Option 1 contradicts "No one need cheat".
options: Researchers deliberately exploit flaws in public test sets.
Benchmarks should be abolished because they encourage cheating.
Fields without benchmarks make faster progress.
Benchmarks are useful but tend to become targets in themselves, so gains on them need independent corroboration.

questions.question: According to the passage, a benchmark's scores can rise without a matching rise in general capability because:
questions.solution: Para 2: the collective search "finds whatever regularities the test happens to contain, including ones unrelated to the general ability". Option 3 contradicts "No one need cheat". Option 2 describes a response, not the cause. Option 4 is not claimed.
options: the collective search adapts methods to regularities specific to the fixed test
benchmarks are replaced too often to be reliable
researchers falsify their results
newer benchmarks are always easier than older ones

questions.question: The author mentions that new benchmarks are built by people "whose sense of what is difficult has itself been shaped by the old one" in order to suggest that:
questions.solution: The remark is a second limitation of frequent replacement: the old benchmark's influence persists through its designers' intuitions. Option 1 is too absolute. Options 2 and 4 are not suggested.
options: new benchmarks are always biased in favour of older methods
the people who build benchmarks are poorly qualified
replacing benchmarks does not fully escape the influence of the benchmarks replaced
benchmarks should be designed by outsiders to the field

questions.question: The author's recommendation that improvements be "corroborated elsewhere" assumes that:
questions.solution: Corroboration only helps if other settings do not share the original test's idiosyncrasies. Option 1 is stronger than needed: different quirks suffice, not none. Option 3 is contradicted; the method "fits poorly with the incentives". Option 2 is too absolute; the author says it is "harder to tell".
options: data gathered later and by other people is free of all quirks
benchmarks always overstate progress
publication incentives will soon change
the quirks of different evaluation settings are unlikely to coincide with those of the original benchmark

questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Cities that plant trees to cool their streets often count trees rather than shade. A sapling and a mature oak count equally in a planting target, yet one shades a parking space and the other a square. Because targets are met in the year of planting and shade arrives decades later, programmes favour quantity and neglect the care that lets trees survive to maturity.
questions.solution: The passage criticises counting trees instead of shade, which skews programmes toward planting rather than care. Option 1 misreads the oak example, option 2 overgeneralises, and option 4 reverses the point.
options: Cities plant too many oak trees and too few saplings.
Urban trees rarely survive to maturity anywhere.
Tree-planting targets that count trees rather than mature shade encourage planting over long-term care.
Shade is less important than tree numbers for cooling streets.

questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

We praise experts for predicting well, but in many fields the best experts are distinguished less by their forecasts than by how quickly they abandon them. A forecaster who revises in the light of new evidence will often look inconsistent to an audience that remembers her earlier view. The public's preference for consistency thus rewards precisely the stubbornness that makes forecasts worse.
questions.solution: The passage has two linked claims: good experts revise quickly, and a public that prizes consistency rewards stubbornness. Only option 3 captures both. Option 1 is not claimed. Options 2 and 4 are unsupported.
options: Experts are generally poor at predicting the future.
Forecasters should never publish their predictions.
Expertise often lies in revising forecasts promptly, but audiences that value consistency penalise this and so reward worse forecasting.
The public remembers forecasts more accurately than experts do.

questions.question:
There is a sentence that is missing in the paragraph below. Read the paragraph and choose the option that best completes it.

A recipe looks like a set of instructions, but it relies heavily on what the cook already knows. "Fry until golden" assumes that the reader can recognise the right shade, smell the moment before burning and adjust the heat without being told. ____ This is why the same recipe can produce very different dishes in different kitchens.
questions.solution: The blank should generalise from the "fry until golden" example and lead to "This is why ... different dishes". Option 1 does this. Option 2 overstates. Options 3 and 4 are off-topic.
options: The written text, in other words, is only the visible part of a much larger body of practical skill.
Recipes are therefore useless to beginners.
Most cooks prefer to work without recipes.
Frying is the most difficult technique in cooking.

questions.question:
There is a sentence that is missing in the paragraph below. Read the paragraph and choose the option that best completes it.

Archives are often imagined as neutral storehouses of the past. Yet every archive is the result of decisions about what to keep, and those decisions are made by people with their own priorities and constraints of space. ____ The historian who reads an archive is therefore reading not only the past but also the judgements of those who curated it.
questions.solution: The blank must link "decisions about what to keep" to "reading ... the judgements of those who curated it". Option 1 bridges exactly. Option 4 introduces accidental loss, not selection. Option 3 is a recommendation the paragraph does not make. Option 2 is irrelevant.
options: What survives tells us as much about the keepers as about the events recorded.
Archivists are usually trained historians themselves.
Historians should rely on oral testimony instead.
Many archives have been destroyed by fire and flood.

questions.question:
Five jumbled sentences related to a topic are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd one out and key in its number.

  1. Most spoken conversations contain long stretches in which nothing new is said.
  2. These stretches, full of greetings, repetitions and agreement, are not wasted.
  3. They signal attention and keep the social connection alive while the speakers think.
  4. Written messages, which strip them away, can therefore feel abrupt even when their content is polite.
  5. Text messages, unlike speech, can be reread and revised several times before they are sent.
questions.solution: Sentences 1–4 form a chain about the social function of redundant talk and its absence in writing. Sentence 5 notes that text can be revised, which is a property of writing but not part of the argument about the social signal lost when redundancy is removed.

questions.question:
Five jumbled sentences related to a topic are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd one out and key in its number.

  1. Insurers price risk by grouping people whose chances of loss are thought to be similar.
  2. Finer data allows ever smaller groups, down in principle to single individuals.
  3. Regulators in some countries forbid insurers from using the results of genetic tests.
  4. At that limit, insurance stops pooling risk and becomes a prediction of each person's own losses.
  5. Those predicted to suffer most would then pay the most, which is the opposite of what pooling was meant to do.
questions.solution: 1 describes grouping, 2 narrows the groups, 4 takes this "to the limit", and 5 draws the consequence. Sentence 3, on regulatory limits on genetic data, is a distractor with the same subject but no role in the argument.

questions.question:
The four sentences below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Enter the sequence of the four numbers (e.g. 2143).

  1. Yet the instruments that would let them do so are themselves expensive to maintain.
  2. Small weather stations run by volunteers once supplied much of the data on local rainfall.
  3. As volunteers have aged and not been replaced, many of those stations have closed.
  4. Agencies now hope to fill the gaps with automated sensors.
questions.solution: 2 introduces volunteer stations; 3 says they have closed; 4 gives the hoped-for replacement; 1 ("Yet ... let them do so") qualifies that hope. 1 needs 4's "Agencies ... hope" for "them".

questions.question:
The five sentences below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Enter the sequence of the five numbers (e.g. 21435).

  1. The difficulty is that a subsidy, once granted, creates a constituency that defends it.
  2. Governments often introduce subsidies as temporary measures to help a new industry find its feet.
  3. The firms that benefit, and the workers they employ, argue that withdrawal would cause hardship.
  4. That is how a temporary measure becomes permanent: not through anyone's design but through the politics of withdrawal.
  5. Officials who planned to end the subsidy then find themselves arguing against the very people they meant to help, and they usually lose.
questions.solution: 2 states the intention; 1 ("The difficulty is") introduces the problem; 3 specifies the constituency; 5 ("then") shows the officials confronting it and losing; 4 ("That is how ...") names the mechanism just described and must close the paragraph. Ending on 5 would leave "That is how" pointing at an argument that is not yet complete.

questions.question: The author's main point is that:
questions.solution: The author lists three conditions and concludes that choice without them yields "the appearance of competition without its substance". Option 4 overstates; "None of this shows that choice is a mistake". Option 1 is not endorsed. Option 2 is one example, not the main point.
options: public services should be run exactly like markets
parents are unable to judge the quality of schools
the benefits of choice depend on conditions that reforms often fail to secure
choice in public services always harms the poor

questions.question: According to the passage, when a popular provider cannot expand, the arrival of new users results in:
questions.solution: Para 3: "the arrival of new users brings congestion rather than reward". The other options are not stated.
options: congestion rather than reward
lower published scores
higher funding for the provider
the departure of existing users to other providers

questions.question: The author would most likely agree that a school-choice scheme in which funding follows pupils but only families with cars can reach the better schools would:
questions.solution: The scheme meets the third condition (funding follows users) but not the second (cost of acting falls unevenly), which the author says "may sort users by circumstance". Option 2 is false. Option 1 ignores the stated access problem. Option 4 is a sweeping judgement the author never makes.
options: fail only because parents cannot judge school quality
satisfy all three conditions for choice to work
risk sorting pupils by circumstance even if providers are rewarded for attracting them
be preferable to having no choice at all in every case

questions.question: The final clause, "may leave those least able to choose with providers that others have abandoned", primarily serves to:
questions.solution: The clause concludes the warning about reforms that lack the conditions, echoing the uneven-cost point in para 3. Option 3 is wrong because the idea was introduced earlier. Options 1 and 2 are unsupported.
options: show that abandoned providers always improve
suggest that choice should be limited to wealthy families
introduce an entirely new argument against choice
point out a distributional cost that can arise when choice is introduced without its supporting conditions

questions.question: According to the passage, the role of the moon in coral spawning is to:
questions.solution: Para 2: "The moon appears to narrow the window to a few nights." Temperature sets the season, darkness sets the hour, and corals cannot see one another.
options: determine the season in which gametes mature
narrow the spawning window to a few nights within the season
allow colonies to see one another
set the hour of release after sunset

questions.question: The statement that spawning on the wrong night "amounts to the same thing" as failing completely implies that:
questions.solution: The colony releases gametes "where few others are present", which for a species depending "on cross-fertilisation" means near-zero success. Option 3 is not stated. Option 2 contradicts the reliance on cross-fertilisation. Option 4 misreads the light point.
options: fertilisation success depends on the presence of gametes from other colonies at the same time
corals can self-fertilise if necessary
the eggs released on the wrong night are biologically defective
artificial light destroys coral gametes

questions.question: The author's concern about warming oceans relies on the assumption that:
questions.solution: Warming "may advance the maturation of gametes" out of step with "the usual lunar window". The worry requires that the lunar cue does not move with temperature. Option 3 is the opposite. Options 1 and 2 are not required.
options: corals will stop responding to darkness
all coral species spawn on the same night
the lunar cycle will itself change as oceans warm
maturation timing and the lunar cue may shift relative to each other because only one responds to temperature

questions.question: The main purpose of the final paragraph is to:
questions.solution: The paragraph notes that the data are "patchy" and then says "if the trend is real, it illustrates a general point". Option 4 overstates. Option 2 is too dismissive. Option 3 contradicts "coordinates without communication".
options: draw a general lesson from tentative evidence of declining synchrony
dismiss reports of changes in spawning as unreliable
explain how corals communicate
prove that coral spawning has become unsynchronised everywhere

questions.question: The passage argues primarily that legal devices for forgetting:
questions.solution: Paras 2–3 argue that limitation and discharge protect people's ability to plan, which is "a deliberate design for the future". Option 2 is the view the author says "misses much of their purpose". Option 1 is not proposed. Option 3 is unsupported.
options: should be abolished in the digital age
exist mainly because evidence becomes unreliable over time
are unique to modern legal systems
serve a forward-looking purpose of allowing people to rely on settled matters and rebuild their lives

questions.question: The author uses the observation that limitation rules apply "even where the evidence is perfectly preserved" to:
questions.solution: If decay were the only reason, the rules would vary by kind of evidence. Their uniformity points to another interest. Option 1 is too strong; the author says decay is not the "only" rationale. Options 2 and 4 are not argued.
options: prove that evidence decay is irrelevant to the law
argue that limitation periods should be lengthened
show that evidence decay cannot be the whole rationale for limitation periods
criticise legal systems for inconsistency

questions.question: According to the passage, discharging a debtor's remaining debt can benefit the wider economy because:
questions.solution: Para 3: forgiveness "gives the debtor a reason to return to productive life". Option 1 overstates "may cost those creditors little". Options 3 and 4 are not stated.
options: creditors receive more money than they otherwise would
the debtor regains an incentive to earn and return to productive life
it removes debts from the official record permanently
it reduces the number of bankruptcy cases

questions.question: Which of the following situations most closely reflects the problem described in the final paragraph?
questions.solution: The final paragraph concerns legal forgetting that wider society undoes through permanent digital records. Option 3 is exactly that. Options 4 and 1 show legal forgetting working. Option 2 is unrelated.
options: A debtor is discharged from bankruptcy and starts a new business.
A company destroys its old financial records after ten years.
A man whose minor conviction was legally expunged keeps losing job offers because employers find old news reports about it online.
A court refuses to hear a claim filed after the limitation period expired.

questions.question: According to the passage, settlements absent from official maps are hard to provide with services because:
questions.solution: Para 2: services "are planned by reference to mapped streets and registered addresses". The other options are not stated.
options: such services are planned by reference to mapped streets and registered addresses
authorities lack the funds to provide services anywhere
residents refuse to cooperate with authorities
informal settlements are always located on dangerous land

questions.question: The author's attitude towards community mapping projects is best described as:
questions.solution: The author agrees that advocates celebrate them "with reason", then warns that "becoming visible carries risks". Options 2 and 3 each ignore one side of that balance. Option 1 contradicts the engaged discussion.
options: indifferent to their outcomes
unreservedly enthusiastic
hostile, because mapping enables eviction
appreciative but alert to the risks of visibility

questions.question: The sentence "A precise map of an informal settlement is also a precise map for anyone who wishes to clear it" serves to:
questions.solution: It illustrates "mapping is not neutral", since information gathered for services can serve eviction. Options 2 and 1 overstate. Option 3 contradicts the sentence, which says "precise".
options: prove that authorities always intend to evict residents
argue that mapping projects should stop
show that maps are usually inaccurate
illustrate how the same information can be used against the people it describes

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the conclusion of the passage?
questions.solution: The final paragraph says the value "depends less on the map itself than on who controls its use" and ends on "on whose terms". Option 2 contradicts "not whether". Option 3 ignores the control issue. Option 1 contradicts the eviction cases.
options: Community mapping always leads to better services.
Poor communities should avoid being mapped.
Official maps should include all informal settlements immediately.
The benefits of being mapped depend largely on who controls how the data are used.

questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Second-hand bookshops survive in towns where new bookshops have closed, partly because their stock costs little and partly because browsing among unpredictable titles offers something online catalogues do not. A buyer who finds a book she was not looking for has had an experience that no recommendation engine can quite reproduce, since such engines suggest what resembles past choices.
questions.solution: The passage gives two reasons for survival: cheap stock and serendipity that engines cannot reproduce. Option 2 overstates, and options 1 and 4 are not claimed.
options: New bookshops close because of second-hand competition.
Recommendation engines are useless for book buyers.
Second-hand bookshops survive through low costs and the value of unplanned discoveries that algorithms do not replicate.
Online catalogues contain fewer titles than second-hand shops.

questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Disasters are often followed by calls to learn their lessons, and inquiries duly produce long lists of recommendations. Yet the organisations that receive them are usually busy with the work that the disaster interrupted, and recommendations compete with daily demands for attention. Lessons are learned on paper long before they are learned in practice, and sometimes they never are.
questions.solution: The essence is the gap between recommendations on paper and practice, explained by competing daily demands. Option 2 is a side note. Option 4 imputes deliberate intent. Option 1 is unsupported.
options: Disasters are usually caused by poor record-keeping.
Inquiries into disasters produce too many recommendations.
Recommendations after disasters are often not put into practice because they compete with organisations' routine demands.
Organisations deliberately ignore inquiry findings.

questions.question:
There is a sentence that is missing in the paragraph below. Read the paragraph and choose the option that best completes it.

A city's skyline is usually read as a record of its ambitions, each tower a statement by a developer or a company. But skylines also record what was forbidden. Height limits around airports, protected views of old buildings and rules about shadows on public parks all leave gaps that are as deliberate as the towers. ____
questions.solution: The paragraph moves from ambition to deliberate gaps; option 4 concludes by joining both. Options 1, 2 and 3 introduce claims the paragraph does not support.
options: Skyscrapers are the most efficient use of urban land.
Airports should be moved further from city centres.
Most cities have abandoned height limits.
To read a skyline fully, one must notice its absences as well as its peaks.

questions.question:
There is a sentence that is missing in the paragraph below. Read the paragraph and choose the option that best completes it.

Surveys that ask people how much they read tend to overstate reading, because respondents know that reading is admired. ____ Researchers who want accurate figures therefore ask about yesterday rather than about a typical week, and about specific titles rather than about reading in general.
questions.solution: The blank must explain why specific, recent questions help: general, flattering questions invite aspirational answers. Option 1 does this. Option 4 contradicts "overstate". Option 2 is off-point. Option 3 contradicts the method described.
options: The more general and flattering the question, the more room it leaves for answers that reflect aspiration rather than habit.
Reading has declined steadily for decades.
Surveys should never ask about cultural activities.
Many people read more than they admit.

questions.question:
Five jumbled sentences related to a topic are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd one out and key in its number.

  1. Bees visiting a flower collect nectar and, incidentally, carry pollen to the next flower.
  2. Some flowers have evolved shapes that only a single species of bee can enter.
  3. The plant gains fertilisation; the bee gains food.
  4. Neither intends to help the other, yet each depends on the exchange.
  5. Such mutualism without intention is common throughout nature.
questions.solution: 1, 3, 4 and 5 describe pollination as unintended mutual benefit and generalise. Sentence 2 concerns specialised flower shapes (co-evolved exclusivity), which is about bees and flowers but not about benefit as an unintended by-product.

questions.question:
Five jumbled sentences related to a topic are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd one out and key in its number.

  1. A footnote can seem a minor feature of scholarly writing.
  2. Yet it allows a reader to check every claim against its source.
  3. Without it, scholarship would rest on trust in the author alone.
  4. Footnotes also give authors a place for digressions that would interrupt the main argument.
  5. The humble footnote is thus one of the foundations of verifiable knowledge.
questions.solution: 1 → 2 → 3 → 5 argues that footnotes enable verification. Sentence 4, on footnotes as a place for digressions, mentions notes but plays no part in the argument.

questions.question:
The four sentences below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Enter the sequence of the four numbers (e.g. 2143).

  1. The result is that scarce supplies reach the people who can travel, not those who most need them.
  2. During shortages, governments often cap the price of essential goods.
  3. Shops then run out quickly, and buyers must queue or travel between them.
  4. The cap is meant to protect poorer households from rising costs.
questions.solution: 2 introduces the cap; 4 gives its aim; 3 ("then") gives the consequence; 1 ("The result") concludes, ironically reversing the aim.

questions.question:
The five sentences below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Enter the sequence of the five numbers (e.g. 21435).

  1. This makes the leaf both a solar panel and a cooling system.
  2. A leaf must open its pores to take in carbon dioxide.
  3. But open pores also let water escape, and in hot weather the loss can be severe.
  4. Plants have evolved to treat this loss as a resource: evaporation cools the leaf.
  5. Whether it can afford to play both roles depends on how much water reaches its roots.
questions.solution: 2 states the need; 3 ("But") gives the cost; 4 recasts the cost as a resource; 1 ("This") names the dual role; 5 ("both roles") adds the constraint.

questions.question: The passage mainly argues that:
questions.solution: Paras 1–3 present boredom as a signal and warn that silencing it costs the reflection it should prompt; para 4 keeps the "information" view. Option 3 is the view challenged. Option 2 is the stronger claim the author doubts. Option 4 is unsupported.
options: boredom is a useful signal whose value is lost when it is immediately silenced
boredom is the main source of human creativity
boredom should be eliminated through better entertainment
psychologists disagree about whether boredom exists

questions.question: According to the passage, boredom is compared to hunger because both:
questions.solution: Para 2: "Like hunger, the signal is unpleasant precisely so that it will be acted upon."
options: disappear when one uses a phone
are caused by lack of food
are more common in the young
are unpleasant in order to prompt action

questions.question: The author's attitude to the claim that boredom is "the mother of creativity" is best described as:
